Most days, the great egret is a rumor of lifeâan ivory figure pinned to the shallows, so still it seems the marsh has grown a statue. You grow accustomed to its vigil, to that disciplined hush of muscle and feather, to the idea that such a creature belongs to water and waiting. And then, on a day that feels briefly unguarded, it breaks its vow of stillness. The long neck uncoils, the white wings unfurl like a sudden thought, and the bird lifts. What was once an emblem of patience becomes pure motionâslow, deliberate, immenseâcrossing the sky with a grandeur made rarer by how seldom it chooses to move.

In this age of vitriol and cruelty, the only path left is kindness. Ask yourself: do you see kindness in Emilyâs celebration of rank elitism, or in the simplicity of a humble bird? Perhaps coolness lies not in hierarchies set in stone by spite and disgust, but in an open presence with gratitude for life even in its most everyday, plain-seeming ways.

The alpine bird wars... eternal and unchanging. Three Clark's Nutcrackers do battle with a swarm of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of finches. The finches are a mixed flock, mostly consisting of Gray-crowned Rosy-Finches and Black Rosy-Finches. Both the Nutcrackers and Rosy-Finches are only spotted at the highest peaks of the Rocky Mountains; this particular bird skirmish is occurring directly in front of the Alta police station and the sheriff is doing absolutely nothing to resolve this disturbance of the bird peace. Before birdfeeders came around, nutcrackers lived on pine nuts, burying them in the summer and using their supreme corvid intellect to retrieve them in the winter. This habit has lead them to develop one of the strongest spatial memories in nature, capable of remembering 6000+ unique caches over the course of a year. Much like squirrels and acorns, this species has developed a mutualistic relationship with whitebark pine, and these birds play an indispensable role in the fight to restore pine in areas decimated by logging and the foul work of the nefarious mountain pine beetle.

Thereâs something quietly unforgettable about seeing a lone wild turkey.

Most of the time, wild turkeys move in flocks â a loose assembly of watchful heads, bronze feathers catching the light, soft clucks and rustles moving through brush together. Thatâs how we expect to see them: communal, alert, almost political in their numbers. So when you come across a single turkey standing alone in a clearing, the moment feels unusual â like youâve stumbled onto a private scene not meant for witnesses.

The bird seems larger by itself. Without others to divide your attention, every detail sharpens: the iridescent sheen of its feathers shifting between copper and green, the deliberate tilt of its head, the long legs built for sudden motion. It carries a strange presence â both awkward and dignified.

And then it runs.

A wild turkey running is one of the most prehistoric sights you can witness in the modern woods. Its body lowers slightly, wings held close, neck stretched forward like a spear. Those powerful legs pump with startling speed, scratching and thudding against earth and leaves. In that instant, the bird stops looking like something from a farmyard and starts looking like something ancient â a survivor from another era. You can almost see the lineage stretching backward through time, feathers transforming into scales, forests thickening into primordial swamps.

There is a dinosaur echo in the way it moves.

That sudden, ground-eating sprint feels older than language. Itâs raw instinct made visible â no grace for an audience, no ceremony. Just motion. Just survival.

Seeing one alone makes it even more striking. Without the distraction of a flock, youâre watching a single thread of evolution flicker across the landscape. A creature that feels both entirely of this moment and impossibly old.

Itâs a special sight not because it is dramatic, but because it is rare and intimate. A lone turkey in the wild feels like a reminder: the ancient world is not gone. It is still here, feathered and wary, running through the trees.

Bigger isnât always better. This is beautifully exemplified by observing the case of the Cedar Waxwing vs. Bald Eagle. These plump tufted guys are small, but boy do they know how to have a good time! On a sunny Sunday afternoon walk, I observed 8-12 Cedar Waxwings fluttering about a tree. With their black bandit mask markings, and lemon yellow tipped tail and tufts, these silly birds are a standout. Upon closer inspection, I could see that they were feasting on hawthorn berries and cheerfully chirping amongst themselves. How sweet is it that these jolly fellas congregate together and get intoxicated from fermented berries! Much like humans, Cedar Waxwings are rarely seen alone as they value community, and often even pass berries down a line from bill to bill. Seeing these little guys embody the importance of community, sharing, and whimsy reminded me to be ever grateful for the friends and family that I have in my own life, and to not take life too seriously.

On the contrary, Bald Eagles are greedy, disloyal, and lazy birds. As described by founding father Benjamin Franklin, the â[Bald Eagle] is a Bird of bad moral Character. He does not get his Living honestly. You may have seen him perched on some dead Tree near the River, where, too lazy to fish for himself, he watches the Labour of the Fishing Hawk (osprey); and when that diligent Bird has at length taken a Fish, and is bearing it to his Nest for the Support of his Mate and young Ones, the Bald Eagle pursues him and takes it from himâ. A founding father of the United States himself did not want the Bald Eagle to be the national bird of the United States, which nullifies my opponents argument. My opponent argues that the Cedar Waxwing âberry goonsâ, but I make the case that at least they are able to forage for their own food, as opposed to thieving from the hard work of others. Countering the third argument made by my opponent of âAuraâ- does my opponent refer to the behavior of Bald Eagles attacking their own kind? Or does he mean the recorded instances of the Bald Eagle eating its own young? Behaviors that a Cedar Waxwing could not fathom. To me, âAuraâ is chirping with friends. It is sharing with one another. It is loving thy neighbor. Although small in size, these vibrant feathered friends represent the interconnectedness of living beings, and how in a way, we are all the Cedar Waxwing.

2) The Bald Eagle frame mogs the Cedar Waxwing with its 7-foot wingspan and massive apex-tier skeletal structure. The medium ugly (more on that later) Cedar Waxwing is merely 12 inches tip to tip. Bald Eagles hit 100mph air speed on a dive, Cedar Waxwings can barely muster 25mph.

Oh it's... a songbird. What could the Northern Shrike or Lanius borealis possibly do to compete? Huh? The family name Lanius is derived from the latin word "butcher"? Why would this grey solitary cousin of a finch be known as the 'butcher bird'? Seems like overkill, no? I mean it weighs as much as a handful of quarters. It doesn't have talons to grip and crush, or the powerful hooked beak of a falcon. The shrike is a grey, unremarkable visitor. The kind of bird that drifts down from the subarctic in winter, sits on a fence post, and gets mistaken for something common. Most people will never notice one.

They should.

The northern shrike hunts prey larger than itself. Other birds, mice, voles, anything with a pulse. Without the standard-issue equipment birds of prey rely on, the northern shrike strikes the cervical vertebrae of its victims, severing the spinal cord in a single blow. Precise. Efficient. Cold.

And because it can't hold its kills the way a raptor does, the shrike finds a thorn, a sharp branch, or barbed wire and impales its prey on it. Ornithologists call this "lardering", I call this "scary shit". A little grey assassin and sociopath with no allies.

The automatic doors parted with a sigh and swallowed me into the fluorescent republic of bulk abundance. Inside Costco, humanity moved in great, squeaking caravans of carts, metal ribs rattling under the weight of paper towels stacked like battlements and jars of olives the size of aquariums. Voices ricocheted off the high raftersâprice checks, arguments over almond versus oat milk, the shriek of a child who had locked eyes with a pallet of inflatable kayaks and recognized destiny. A man rehearsed his authority into his phone. A woman laughed like a startled jay. Someone whistled to locate a wandering spouse. The bakery exhaled sugar and yeast into the bright air.

It struck me how avian it all was. The darting glances, the territorial edging of carts, the way people clustered around the sample stations as if around a feeder newly filled. Hands flicked and peckedâgrapes sampled, crackers snapped, napkins abandoned like shed feathers. Even the ceiling fans seemed to circle overhead like patient hawks. We were a murmuration constrained by aisles, our choreography dictated by signage and sale tags, our calls overlapping into a single, restless canopy of sound.

When I finally escaped with my receipt slashed in blue ink, the outside air felt tidal and honest. The parking lot shimmered. And there, by the concrete bollards near the food court, a small parliament of Western gull had convened around a fallen treasure: a chicken bake torn open, steam still ghosting from its breaded flank.

They were magnificent and ridiculous. White chests puffed with outrage, slate wings lifted like capes, yellow bills jabbing with courtroom precision. One gull seized the prize and bolted; another clipped it mid-stride; a third shrieked commentary from the sidelines. The sound was not unlike the interior weâd just leftâsharp, insistent, threaded with grievance. A gull threw its head back and loosed a cry that could have been, to an inattentive ear, âMine!â Another answered with a scold that echoed the tone of a price dispute at the register.

Watching them, I felt the hinge between species loosen. Their skirmish replayed the choreography of the warehouse: the rush toward abundance, the flare of entitlement, the quick arithmetic of appetite. 

In the end, the chicken bake surrendered to entropyâcrumbs scattered, a victor crowned only briefly before being dethroned by gravity and greed. The gulls lifted in a sudden, unanimous updraft, their wings beating the air into order. For a moment the parking lot was quiet again, carts ticking as they cooled.
Inside, we had been birds pretending to be civilized. Outside, the birds were people without the pretense. And somewhere between the receipt and the sky, the mimicry felt mutual: our racket answering theirs, their hunger mirroring ours, each species fluent in the bright, unruly grammar of want.

Nearing the end of my leisurely neighborhood walk, a dark shape against the bright blue sky caught my eye. A hawk! Its four-foor-wide wings outstretched, it soared silently before alighting on the very top of a huge Ponderosa pine. The call of a red-tailed hawk is used for that of a bald eagle in movies, TV shows, advertisements, and endless other pieces of aural Americana. Wherever bald eagles rank on the here of cool, red-tailed hawks are well above them. Red-tailed hawks are sexually dimorphic: females are up to 25% larger than males (extremely cool). Finally, red-tailed hawks are truly an apex predator; indeed, some of the birds that have been submitted to Bird League in weeks past - namely gulls and rock pigeons - are prey for red-tailed hawks. On that normal day, on my normal walk, I suddenly felt awe as was due such a creature. As swiftly as it had appeared, the hawk launched into the air and winged her way toward the horizon.

'Snow' goose in the middle of the Chihuahua desert? Strange but true! In El Paso we spotted this juvenile, a very rare sighting for the region, even as the Snow Goose tends to overwinter in warmer climates. Rarer still, he was the only goose in the area. Those aren't fellow geese behind him, they're seagulls. Where did the rest of his flock go? This young goose seemed to be doing well for himself, but what drove him to strike it out on his own? American culture has long had a fascination with the "lone wolf" archetype, but rarer and even more compelling is the "lone goose" archetype this mysterious specimen embodies.

For most of my life, I carried a quiet awareness of my nose. In mirrors, in photos, in the small pauses before meeting someone new, I felt it arrive before the rest of me. I learned angles, lighting, little habits of turning my face just so. It wasnât shame exactlyâmore like a constant whisper reminding me that I didnât quite match the picture I thought I was supposed to.

Then one day I noticed the American white ibis.

There it was, walking calmly along the waterâs edge, white feathers bright in the sun, and that impossibly long, curved bill leading the way. It didnât hide it. It didnât apologize. The bill was the very thing that let it search the mud, find food, live fully in the place it belonged.

Watching it, something loosened in me.

Maybe the features we worry about are not mistakes but tools for being exactly who we are. Maybe what stands out is simply what helps us move through the world in our own way.

Now when I step outside, I think of that ibisâunbothered, purposeful, unmistakable.

And for the first time, I feel a little more like stepping forward just as I am.
